prompt: Order the steps from password to session.
steps: The customer submits credentials over HTTPS
The server verifies them and creates a session record
The server's Set-Cookie header gives the browser a random session ID
A later request carries the ID in its Cookie header
The server looks up the session, checks it is valid, then checks permission
explanation: Later requests use the session ID rather than resending the password. The ID does not let the browser choose its own role.

prompt: Match each cookie setting to its purpose.

pairs.match: Send the cookie only over HTTPS
Stop ordinary page JavaScript reading the cookie
Limit when the cookie is sent with requests started by other sites

explanation: Cookie settings reduce exposure of the session ID. They do not replace the server's access checks.

prompt: Each account has an `id` and a `role`. Each purchase has an `ownerId`. Which function body correctly implements "the owner, or any support staff member, may view a purchase"?

options.text: `if (!account || !purchase) return false; return account.id === purchase.ownerId || account.role === "support";`
`if (!account || !purchase) return false; return account.id === purchase.id || account.role === "support";`
options.why: `purchase.id` is the order's own ID, not the owner's, so this compares the wrong values.

options.text: `if (!account || !purchase) return false; return account.id === purchase.ownerId && account.role === "support";`
options.why: `&&` requires the person to be both the owner and support, so owners are refused.

options.text: `return Boolean(account && purchase);`
options.why: This only checks that both records exist; anyone signed in could view any purchase.

explanation: `purchase.id` is the order's own ID, not the owner's, so comparing it with `account.id` is wrong. Using `&&` would require the requester to be both the owner and support. `Boolean(account && purchase)` only checks that both records exist.

prompt: This function decides whether an account may view a purchase. What happens if the `||` on the last line is replaced with `&&`?

options.text: Only someone who is both the owner and a support staff member gets access
Nothing changes, because both operators check the same things
options.why: `&&` and `||` differ: `||` needs either condition, `&&` needs both.

options.text: Everyone is allowed, because && is less strict than || here
options.why: `&&` is stricter, not looser: both conditions must be true.

options.text: Owners are allowed, but support staff are always denied
options.why: Owners are the ones refused: an owner who isn't also support staff fails, because `&&` needs both conditions.

explanation: `||` allows either condition: the owner, or support staff. `&&` would require both at once, so ordinary owners and support staff viewing other people's purchases would all be denied.

prompt: Horizontal or vertical access failure?

pairs.item: One customer reads another customer's order
pairs.why: Same privilege level, someone else's data.

pairs.item: A customer issues a refund, which only support staff may do
pairs.why: Gaining a function reserved for a higher role.

pairs.item: One customer edits another customer's delivery address
pairs.why: Same privilege level, someone else's data.

pairs.item: A customer opens an admin-only export page
pairs.why: Gaining a function reserved for a higher role.

explanation: Horizontal: same privilege level, someone else's data. Vertical: gaining a higher-privilege function.

prompt: An online shop's policy: a customer may read only their own orders. Support staff may read any order and may issue refunds. Customers may not issue refunds, even on their own orders. Requests without a valid session are refused. Sam owns order 101 and Priya owns order 102. Should each request be allowed or denied?

pairs.why: Customers may read only their own orders.
Owners may read their own orders.

pairs.item: Priya (customer) issues a refund on her own order 102
pairs.why: Refunds are support-only, even for the owner.

pairs.item: A support staff member reads Sam's order 101
pairs.why: Support staff may read any order.

pairs.item: A support staff member issues a refund on Sam's order 101
A request with no valid session reads order 101
pairs.why: No valid session means no identity to check, so refuse.

explanation: Reading depends on ownership or the support role. Issuing a refund is a separate, support-only action, so owning the order is not enough. With no valid session there is no identity to check, so the request is refused.

prompt: Hiding the refund button from customers prevents them issuing refunds.
explanation: A direct request to the refund endpoint still works unless the server checks the requester's role before changing anything.

prompt: Replacing sequential document IDs with random values would, on its own, fix a missing access check.
explanation: Less predictable IDs reduce guessing, but known IDs still need a permission check for each requested document.

prompt: A user is signed in to the shop. For each cross-site case, does the browser send the shop session cookie? (Assume the SameSite value is set explicitly.)
text: A link on another site takes the user to the shop with a normal top-level GET. With SameSite=Strict the cookie is [[not sent|sent]]. With SameSite=Lax it is [[sent|not sent]]. Another site submits a form POST to the shop. With SameSite=Lax the cookie is [[not sent|sent]]. Another site shows the shop inside an iframe. With SameSite=Lax the cookie is [[not sent|sent]].
explanation: With None; Secure, cross-site POST and iframe requests are eligible, subject to browser third-party-cookie restrictions.

prompt: An origin is the scheme, host and port together. A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain (here example.com). How does each URL relate to https://shop.example.com?

pairs.why: Only the path differs, so scheme, host and port all match.
A different subdomain changes the origin but keeps the registrable domain.
A different port changes the origin but not the site.
Changing HTTPS to HTTP changes the scheme, so it's a different site.

explanation: A different path keeps the origin. A different subdomain or port changes the origin but keeps the site. Changing HTTPS to HTTP changes the schemeful site.

prompt: HttpOnly stops page scripts reading the cookie, but it does not prevent cross-site scripting.
explanation: HttpOnly stops ordinary page JavaScript reading the cookie, but injected script can still make the browser send authenticated requests.

prompt: What is cross-site request forgery (CSRF)?

options.text: Another site makes the browser send an unwanted request using the user's cookie
An attacker steals the user's session cookie using script injected into the page
options.why: Stealing a cookie with injected script is XSS, not CSRF.

options.text: A signed-in user changes an ID in the URL to read someone else's record
options.why: Changing an ID to read another record is broken access control.

options.text: A server sends back more fields in its response than the page actually needs
options.why: Returning extra fields is excessive data exposure.

explanation: Use framework CSRF tokens and origin checks, keep state changes off GET, and treat SameSite as one layer. Sibling domains can be same-site, and CORS is not a universal CSRF defence.

prompt: Match each OWASP API authorisation failure to the question it fails to answer.

pairs.match: May this user access this particular record?
Which fields of the record may this user read or change?
May this user perform this action, such as issuing a refund?

explanation: Check the record, the fields and the action separately, on the server.

prompt: A customer who owns order 101 changes the request /api/orders/101 to /api/orders/102. Input validation confirms 102 is a correctly formed order number. What does that establish?

options.text: Only that the ID is well formed, not that access is allowed
That the customer is allowed to read order 102 as well
options.why: A well-formed ID doesn't mean the customer owns or may read that order.

options.text: That the request is a cross-site request forgery attack
options.why: Changing an ID yourself isn't a cross-site request; it's an access control test.

options.text: That order 102 must belong to the same customer as 101
options.why: Order numbers don't imply ownership; 102 belongs to whoever placed it.

explanation: An identifier tells the server which object is targeted, not who may access it.

prompt: Which cookie settings are a sensible starting point for an ordinary shop's session cookie?

options.text: Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
SameSite=None without Secure
options.why: SameSite=None requires Secure, and without it the browser rejects the cookie.

options.text: HttpOnly only
options.why: Without Secure the cookie can travel over HTTP, and without SameSite it is sent cross-site more freely.

options.text: Secure; SameSite=None; Domain=.example
options.why: None with a broad Domain widens exposure; an ordinary shop doesn't need cross-site sending.

explanation: Lax lets a normal incoming link keep the session. Consider Strict for tighter isolation, and None; Secure only for a genuine cross-site need.

prompt: A refund endpoint only checks that the requester is signed in. What is the consequence?

options.text: Every authenticated customer could issue refunds
Only support staff can issue refunds, as intended
options.why: Nothing restricts refunds to support; any signed-in customer passes the check.

options.text: No one at all can issue refunds, including support
options.why: Signed-in users can issue refunds, so it isn't nobody.

options.text: Refunds are limited to the customer who owns the order
options.why: The check doesn't look at ownership or role at all.

explanation: Check `account.role === "support"` from trusted records before recording a refund or changing the order.

prompt: A valid session ID works like a password. Which of these places would expose it? Select all that apply.

options.text: A URL
A screenshot shared with other people
An application log
The Cookie header of a request sent over HTTPS
options.why: The Cookie header is the intended way for the session ID to travel, and HTTPS protects it on the way.

explanation: The Cookie header is how the session ID is meant to travel. Keep it out of URLs, screenshots and logs, and renew it when authentication or privilege changes.

prompt: What is the attack called when another site tricks a signed-in user's browser into sending an unintended state-changing request?
explanation: Use framework CSRF tokens, origin checks where appropriate, and keep state changes off GET. SameSite is a useful extra layer.

prompt: A shop's session cookie uses SameSite=Lax. Why should its refund endpoint still not accept GET requests?

options.text: Lax still sends the cookie when a user follows a normal link from another site
Lax blocks every GET request, so the refund endpoint would never work
options.why: Lax doesn't block GET; it sends the cookie on normal top-level links.

options.text: GET requests can't carry cookies, so the user wouldn't be signed in
options.why: GET requests can carry cookies, which is exactly the risk.

options.text: Refund details are too large to fit into the URL of a GET request
options.why: Size isn't the reason; the danger is a link triggering a refund.

explanation: Keep changes off GET and keep CSRF protection for state-changing requests.

prompt: When a user clicks Log out, what must the server do so that a previously captured session ID stops working?

options.text: Delete or invalidate the session record on the server
Tell the browser to delete the cookie, and nothing else
options.why: A copy of the ID captured earlier would still match a live session on the server.

options.text: Redirect the user straight back to the login page
options.why: A redirect changes the page shown; it doesn't end the server-side session.

options.text: Change the cookie's SameSite setting to Strict
options.why: SameSite controls cross-site sending; it doesn't end the session.

explanation: A session ID works like a password for the life of the session. Invalidate it on the server, then also clear the browser's copy.
